text: Every quantum gate you'll study in future courses — Hadamard, CNOT, the Pauli gates — is, physically, a unitary matrix. This lesson makes the connection explicit: gates ARE time evolution, and unitarity is a physical necessity, not a design choice.

Solving the Schrödinger equation for a fixed Hamiltonian produces a specific unitary matrix for each duration. Building a gate physically means the reverse: starting from the matrix you want, then engineering a Hamiltonian and a duration so that the resulting evolution matches it exactly. Applying the Hadamard gate to a real qubit means literally letting it sit under a specifically engineered Hamiltonian for a calibrated amount of time — there's no other mechanism. A gate is a particular instance of the same time evolution covered the last three lessons, chosen on purpose.

Three verified facts tie this together. Hadamard times Hadamard equals the identity — it's its own inverse. Pauli-X times Pauli-X equals the identity — a bit-flip applied twice returns the original. And the S gate, squared, equals Pauli-Z, since i times i is negative 1, matching Z's second diagonal entry exactly. These aren't convenient bookkeeping identities — they're statements about what happens when you let the corresponding physical system evolve for exactly twice the duration of a single gate.

A matrix that isn't unitary cannot correspond to any valid stretch of Schrödinger-equation evolution under any Hamiltonian, full stop — unitarity is exactly the condition that keeps total probability equal to 1 at every moment. A non-unitary gate would mean probability drifting away from 1 over time, which isn't a worse gate, it's a mathematical impossibility for a closed quantum system. That's why every gate in every real circuit specification is unitary.

Because every unitary matrix has an inverse, every quantum gate is reversible — you can always recover the input exactly from the output. Classical AND and OR gates are generally not reversible; you can't always recover both inputs from the output. Quantum circuits, built entirely from unitary operations, never lose information this way mid-circuit — the only place information is genuinely thrown away is at measurement, a fundamentally different kind of step.
